title: Resonance and damping
summary: A driven, damped oscillator: one linear equation, one resonance peak, and a phase that always crosses a quarter turn exactly at omega_0. Turn the drive up far enough on the pendulum toggle and the peak folds over — the point where the linear analytic curve stops describing the sim.
question: Drive the oscillator exactly at its natural frequency omega_0. Does the amplitude grow without bound, settle to a fixed value, or beat forever without settling — and what sets how long it takes to get there?
prediction_prompt: Predict before you touch a control:

prediction_options.label: Driving exactly at omega_0 always makes the amplitude grow without bound, however much damping there is.
prediction_options.feedback: Watch the light-damping-at-resonance preset run to completion: x(t) grows for a while and then settles onto a fixed envelope ±A(omega_0) = ±F/(2 zeta). Only the undamped limit (zeta = 0) truly diverges at exact resonance.

prediction_options.label: It settles to a steady amplitude set by the damping; less damping means a larger steady amplitude and a longer settling time.
prediction_options.feedback: This is what the runs show: the steady-state amplitude at resonance is F/(2 zeta omega_0) = F Q / omega_0, and the transient envelope e^{-zeta omega_0 t} decays on the timescale 1/(zeta omega_0) -- lighter damping means both a bigger peak and a slower approach to it.

prediction_options.label: It grows, then beats forever without ever settling down, however long you wait.
prediction_options.feedback: Beating (a slowly modulated envelope that never dies out) is what an undamped oscillator does when driven off resonance. With any damping (zeta > 0) at exact resonance, the transient simply decays and the motion settles onto the steady state -- compare with the off-resonance-beats preset, where the modulation you see is the transient dying out, not a permanent beat.

model.summary: A unit-mass, unit-natural-frequency oscillator with linear viscous damping, driven by a sinusoidal force: x'' + 2*zeta*omega_0*x' + omega_0^2*x = F cos(omega t). The 'pendulum' toggle replaces the linear restoring term omega_0^2*x with sin(x) -- the same nonlinearity in the pendulum-driven starter this chapter extends -- to show where the linear analytic model this page validates stops describing the motion.
model.units: Dimensionless: omega_0 = 1 sets the time scale, so the drive frequency omega, the damping ratio zeta = gamma/omega_0, and the drive amplitude F are all given in these units. Integrated with RK4 (_lib/web/integrators.js, unmodified) over the autonomous state [x, ẋ, t] so the time-dependent drive term needs no special-casing; the step dt = 0.01 used for the validation grid is far inside RK4's stability region for this stiffness (dt << 1/omega_0).

equations.name: Equation of motion
equations.note: linear model; the pendulum toggle replaces ω₀²x with sin(x)

equations.name: Steady-state amplitude
equations.note: the particular solution's amplitude, x_p(t) = A cos(ωt − φ)

equations.name: Steady-state phase lag
equations.note: φ = π/2 exactly at ω = ω₀, regardless of ζ

equations.name: Resonance peak frequency
equations.note: real only for ζ < 1/√2 ≈ 0.707; above that A(ω) decreases monotonically and has no interior peak

equations.name: Quality factor
equations.note: peak amplitude at resonance is F·Q/ω₀; bandwidth Δω/ω₀ ≈ 1/Q for high Q

equations.name: Damped natural frequency
equations.note: underdamped only, ζ < 1; the transient's own oscillation frequency

equations.name: Transient, from rest (underdamped)
equations.text: x(t) = A cos(ωt − φ) + e^{−ζω₀t}[C₁cos(ω_d t) + C₂sin(ω_d t)]
equations.note: C₁, C₂ fixed by x(0) = 0, ẋ(0) = 0; the closed form reference.py and resonance.js both evaluate

equations.name: Power balance at steady state
equations.note: the drive supplies exactly what viscous damping removes, once the transient has died out

assumptions: Linear viscous damping only: the damping force is exactly −2ζω₀ẋ, proportional to velocity. Dry (Coulomb) friction or velocity-squared drag would change both the transient shape and the resonance curve.
The linear restoring force ω₀²x is exact only for small displacement; the pendulum toggle shows the sin(x) alternative without changing anything else.
The drive is a pure sinusoid at a single frequency omega, applied from t = 0 with the system at rest.
Unit mass, unit natural frequency: every quantity here is dimensionless and scales out of a system with different mass or spring constant.

controls.label: drive frequency ω/ω₀
controls.description: Ratio of the drive frequency to the natural frequency. 1.0 is exact resonance.

controls.label: damping ratio ζ
controls.description: γ/ω₀. Below 1: underdamped (oscillatory transient). 1: critically damped. Above 1: overdamped.

controls.label: drive amplitude F
controls.description: Force per unit mass driving the oscillator. Steady-state amplitude scales linearly with F in the linear model; the pendulum model folds over at large F.

controls.label: restoring force

options.label: linear (ω₀²x) — the model this page validates
pendulum (sin x) — nonlinear, no analytic curve

controls.description: Swaps the linear restoring term for sin(x) (the pendulum-driven starter's own nonlinearity), so the drawn oscillator and x(t) still run, but the analytic response curve and validation table stop applying.

presets.label: Light damping at resonance
presets.note: ω = ω₀, ζ = 0.02: the largest steady amplitude this page can show, A = F/(2ζ) = 5F, and the slowest settling time, ~1/ζ = 50 time units.

presets.label: Heavy damping
presets.note: ζ = 1.2 (overdamped): no oscillatory transient at all, x(t) creeps up to the steady state monotonically.

presets.label: Off-resonance beats
presets.note: ω = 0.8 ω₀, ζ = 0.01: the drive and the lightly damped natural response briefly interfere before the transient decays, producing a beat-like envelope on the way to the (much smaller, off-resonance) steady state.

presets.label: Critically damped
presets.note: ζ = 1: the boundary between an oscillatory and a monotonic transient; ω_d = 0 so the closed-form underdamped transient above no longer applies exactly at this point.

presets.label: Nonlinear foldover (large drive)
presets.note: Switches to the pendulum toggle with a large F near resonance: the amplitude-dependent frequency of a real pendulum bends the response away from the linear A(ω) curve, which this preset deliberately drives past.

explanation.heading: Transient versus steady state
body: Starting from rest, x(t) is the sum of two pieces: a steady-state term A cos(ωt − φ) that oscillates forever at the drive frequency, and a transient e^{−ζω₀t}[C₁cos(ω_d t) + C₂sin(ω_d t)] that oscillates near the system's own damped natural frequency ω_d and decays away. Watch the envelope plot: the dashed transient envelope ±e^{−ζω₀t} shrinks toward zero while the dotted steady-state envelope ±A(ω) stays fixed, and x(t) converges onto the steady-state curve once the transient is gone.

explanation.heading: Why damping bounds the resonance peak
body: At exact resonance (ω = ω₀) the two terms in A(ω)'s denominator that would otherwise cancel — (ω₀² − ω²) — vanish exactly, leaving A(ω₀) = F/(2ζω₀). Undamped (ζ → 0) that diverges; any nonzero damping caps it. The lighter the damping, the higher and narrower the peak: Q = 1/(2ζ) is both the peak's height in units of the ω → 0 amplitude and (for high Q) the ratio ω₀/Δω of the resonance frequency to its bandwidth.

explanation.heading: The phase always crosses π/2 at ω₀
body: φ(ω) climbs from near 0 (drive far below resonance, response in phase with the force) through exactly π/2 at ω = ω₀ (response and force in quadrature) to near π (drive far above resonance, response out of phase) — and that midpoint crossing happens at ω₀ regardless of how much damping there is. Only the steepness of the climb depends on ζ: light damping crosses π/2 almost as a step, heavy damping crosses it gradually.

explanation.heading: Energy balance at steady state
body: Once the transient is gone, the average power the drive supplies over a cycle, ⟨P_in⟩ = ½FAω sin φ, exactly equals the average power viscous damping removes, ⟨P_dissipated⟩ = γω²A² (both reduce to the same expression using A(ω) and φ(ω) above). That balance is why the amplitude stops changing: any momentary excess of input over dissipation would have to show up as a change in the stored energy ½ẋ² + ½ω₀²x², and at steady state there isn't one.

explanation.heading: Where the linear model stops applying
body: The pendulum toggle replaces ω₀²x with sin(x) — exact for small x, but sin(x) < x for any nonzero x, so a real pendulum's effective stiffness (and therefore its natural frequency) drops as its amplitude grows. Drive it hard enough (the foldover preset) and the response curve bends over and develops a fold: for a range of ω, three amplitudes solve the steady-state equation instead of one, and which one the pendulum actually settles into depends on history (hysteresis) rather than on ω alone. None of that is on the analytic A(ω)/φ(ω) curve this page validates — the curve and the validation table are drawn for the linear model only, and the pendulum toggle is deliberately left off that curve to make the difference visible rather than papering over it.

Real damping is rarely exactly linear in velocity either: dry (Coulomb) friction and quadratic (velocity-squared) drag both give a different transient shape and a different (non-Lorentzian) resonance curve; neither is modelled here.

validation_cases.description: The predefined validation grid. reference.py integrates every (ω, ζ) point in float64 with numpy available, measures the RK4 steady-state amplitude and phase by demodulating the last few drive cycles at the drive frequency, checks the RK4 trajectory against the closed-form transient throughout the run, and writes validation.json. The browser re-runs the same points in this page through resonance.js and the table reports the difference.

steady_state_tolerance.rationale: Amplitude is compared relatively (0.5%) and phase absolutely (0.005 rad ≈ 0.29°) because phase passes through values close to zero where a relative comparison is unstable; both are RK4-vs-analytic discretisation error, distinct from the browser-vs-Python tolerance below.

tolerance.rationale: resonance.js and reference.py run the same RK4 algorithm in the same operation order in float64, so the two implementations agree bit for bit in practice (observed worst relative difference 0). The declared tolerance is 1e-9 to leave room for a legitimate difference in summation order or in a future JIT's use of fused multiply-add; anything larger is a real disagreement and fails the chapter's kill condition.

limits: Linear damping and linear restoring force only (unless the pendulum toggle is on, which trades the closed-form model for a qualitative one): the analytic A(ω), φ(ω), ω_r and Q above assume both are exact, and the validation grid only checks the linear model.

Nonlinear pendulum (large amplitude, large F): sin(x) ≈ x fails as x grows, the effective natural frequency drops with amplitude, and the response curve folds over with hysteresis instead of tracing a single-valued A(ω) — the toggle shows this qualitatively but this page draws no analytic curve for it.

The closed-form transient above is the underdamped (ζ < 1) solution only; at ζ = 1 (critical) and ζ > 1 (overdamped) the transient has a different closed form (repeated or two real roots) that this page does not evaluate, though the RK4 simulation still runs correctly through those regimes.

Non-viscous damping (dry friction, velocity-squared drag) is not modelled: real damping is often only approximately linear in velocity, and both the transient shape and the resonance curve would differ under a different damping law.
A single drive frequency from t = 0 at rest: no frequency sweep, no multiple simultaneous drives, and no noise.
